headline: High: ECC’s filesystem/MCP-heavy defaults can collide with TREK’s collaborative, secret-bearing workspace, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and action-cascade risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads/writes local files, uses MCP, and treats skills as a primary workflow surface; TREK is real-time collaborative and also exposes MCP/WebSocket surfaces. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if TREK content is fed into ECC or shared files. The interaction is inferred from docs, not directly observed, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF TREK content is copied into ECC-managed files or MCP inputs
IF either agent parses shared workspace text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces for ECC and TREK
Disable or restrict MCP connectors for shared content
Add provenance tags to imported notes and prompts
Review any copied TREK output before ECC consumes it

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, hooks, git history, and security findings, while TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, API keys, and MFA secrets. Both have filesystem and network surfaces, so a shared workspace or account could expose sensitive TREK data through ECC’s broader local state handling. Because the pairwise leakage path is plausible but not directly evidenced, high is safer than medium.
conditions: IF ECC and TREK share a filesystem or synced workspace
IF TREK secrets or documents are opened in ECC-managed paths
IF either agent logs or indexes imported files
mitigations: Keep TREK secrets out of ECC-managed directories
Rotate API keys after any shared-workspace test
Audit logs for copied reservations or MFA material
Use separate OS accounts or containers
Restrict file sync on ./data and ~/.claude-related paths

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; TREK is collaborative and stores mutable travel.db/uploads/logs. Even without explicit locking details, overlapping write authority on shared resources can cause clobbering or inconsistent state. Uncertainty about orchestration and locking pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or repository
IF TREK database/files are edited while ECC runs git or file mutations
IF no external lock or transaction boundary is enforced
mitigations: Assign separate writable directories
Pause one agent during the other’s write phase
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Back up travel.db before concurrent edits
Avoid concurrent git operations in ECC

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s skills/subagents and TREK’s real-time collaborative planner both suggest automation pipelines where one agent’s output may be reused by the other. If TREK consumes ECC-generated facts or plans without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect reservations or travel decisions. The docs imply the pathway, but do not prove direct trust, so medium fits.
conditions: IF TREK ingests ECC-generated plans or facts as authoritative
IF ECC forwards TREK outputs into downstream actions without validation
IF either agent auto-executes browser/API actions from the other’s text
mitigations: Require human review before bookings or commits
Add validation checks between agents
Limit ECC output to drafts, not final actions
Log source provenance for every transferred fact

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles reservations, documents, photos, country visit history, and MFA secrets, while ECC handles session summaries, security findings, and git history. If EU travel data or identity documents flow into ECC’s broader local state or logs, retention and residency obligations may diverge. The profiles do not specify jurisdictions, so I avoid high and keep medium for a plausible policy mismatch.
conditions: IF regulated travel documents or identity data are stored in ECC session files or logs
IF retention settings differ between ECC and TREK for the same records
IF cross-border data is processed without a documented DPA or residency control
mitigations: Separate regulated data from ECC session storage
Set explicit retention limits in both systems
Review where logs and backups are stored
Document data-processing roles for each agent
Delete copied documents after use
